title: The world is too much with us
word: The world is too much with us
hookLine: on a hill above the moonlit sea, Wordsworth cries that getting and spending has cost us our hearts
tomorrow: where were you before you were born? a poet had a guess.

lines: WE HAVE GIVEN OUR HEARTS AWAY.
cards: A full cart. A countdown on the sale. A card number already saved.
Now a man stands in a meadow, a pleasant lea, by the sea. The moon is up, and the wind has dropped, gathered in like sleeping flowers before it howls again.

And he's furious, not at the sea but at himself and everyone he knows: "The world is too much with us; late and soon, / Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers; / Little we see in Nature that is ours; / We have given our hearts away, a sordid boon!"

teach.b: Given away for what? For the getting and the spending. The world here isn't nature.
It's the busy round of buying, earning, owing, and nature is the thing we've stopped seeing. The sea bares herself to the moon, the poem says, and we are not moved.
Then comes a line that still startles, from a Christian poet: "Great God! I'd rather be / A Pagan suckled in a creed outworn".
He'd rather be an old pagan who could see Proteus rising from the sea, or hear Triton blow his wreathed horn, than a modern man who sees nothing at all. That isn't a conversion.
It's a shout of shame: even a creed he called outworn saw the sea as alive.

Some readers hear an older teaching underneath, from the Sermon on the Mount: "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth", Jesus says, "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."
That's the Christian teaching about treasure: the heart follows what you store up.
Wordsworth's sonnet says we've already made the trade.
Our hearts went where our getting went. And the cost isn't only money. It's the power to see, and to be moved.
The sonnet doesn't ask anyone to hate money. It asks us to notice the trade.

how: Many Christians read the Sermon on the Mount's teaching on treasure (Matthew 6) as a call to simplicity, and some keep fasts from spending in Lent.

games.q: what does “the world is too much with us” mean?
o: a cry that busy getting and spending dulls the heart
a promise that the earth will always be with us
a complaint that the planet is too crowded today

games.q: the market and the sea: tap the pairs.
p: an old sea god rising from the waves
a sea god blowing his wreathed horn
a shabby bargain: our hearts given away
there will your heart be also

s: in the title, the world means nature
the world is the busy round of getting and spending; nature is what we've stopped seeing.
the sonnet says getting and spending lays waste our powers
and little we see in Nature that is ours.
Wordsworth's sonnet announces that he has become a pagan
he says he'd rather be one: a shout of shame that even an outworn creed saw the sea as alive.

games.q: a coworker says shopping is how she unwinds, and asks if that's bad. what fits Wordsworth's sonnet?
o: its worry is the trade: whether getting and spending leaves room to see and be moved.
it says every purchase is a sin, so she should stop buying things entirely.
it only criticizes the very rich; ordinary shopping isn't its concern.
games.why: the sonnet's cost is the heart and the power to see: we have given our hearts away. it doesn't ban buying; it names the bargain.

practice: Open the cart, the wishlist, or the list in your head of the next thing you mean to buy. Pick one item, and for two minutes just look at it and ask what you'd be trading for it, in money and in attention.
If you decide to let it go, let it go gently.

wordCard.voice: The world is too much with us: Wordsworth's sonnet against getting and spending. The world is the market; the sea is what we've stopped seeing.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: getting and spending, and what it quietly costs the heart. Back tomorrow.
